t: Minimize Length of Array Using Operations
o: Each operation replaces two positive elements a,b with a%b (net length −1); minimize final length. Two facts drive everything: (1) if some pair produces a nonzero remainder smaller than both (i.e., larger % smaller ≠ 0), a Euclid-style descent can shrink the array to a single element → answer 1; (2) if every element is a multiple of the minimum m, all remainders are 0 or ≥ m, and the only obstacle is having too many copies of m: non-min elements can each be deleted (x % bigger = x when a smaller meets a larger... specifically small % large = small removes the large), but surplus copies of m must be paired into zeros. If c = count(m) and 2c > n, the stranded count is 2c − n, giving ceil((2c−n)/2); otherwise the answer is 1. Examples: [1,4,3,1]→1, [5,5,5,10,5]→2, [2,3,4]→1.
k: larger % smaller ≠ 0 somewhere ⇒ answer 1 via Euclidean descent.
Otherwise all elements are multiples of m; only excess copies of m (when 2c > n) force extra survivors.
Final answer: 1, or ceil((2·count(min) − n)/2) when count(min) > n/2.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct formula from the two cases
a.i: Check whether any element has a nonzero remainder mod the minimum. If yes, answer 1. Otherwise count minimums c; if 2c ≤ n the surplus is absorbable → 1, else ceil((2c−n)/2).
s: Find m = min and c = its count
Return max(1, ceil((2c − n)/2)) — i.e., (2c − n + 1)//2 when 2c > n, else 1

a.i: Classify operations: 'deletion' (a % b = a with a < b removes b for free) and 'zeroing' (equal or dividing pair makes a dead 0). Show any non-minimum element is deletable using the minimum, so only surplus minimums survive; pairing them yields the same formula. Present as reasoning plus the same implementation — useful when asked WHY the formula holds.
s: Argue each non-min element can be eliminated via min % x = min
Remaining c′ = max(0, 2c − n) minimums pair up: each pair → one 0

w: This is a brain-teaser, not a coding problem — spend interview time proving the two cases. Pitfalls: n = 1 (answer 1), arrays where all values are equal (pure pairing → ceil(n/2), which the formula reproduces since c = n gives ceil(n/2)), and forgetting that a % b = a when a < b enables free deletions. Follow-up: what if zeros could also participate in operations?
